skill.name: using-superpowers
skill.description: Guides assistants to check for relevant skills, invoke them before task work, and follow skill-specific workflows.
skill.summary: Standardizes how assistants discover, prioritize, and apply skills during a conversation.
skill.author: sickn33

security_audit.summary: The two static external command findings are false positives caused by markdown inline code and a DOT diagram. No executable code, shell invocation, network access, or filesystem operation is present. A high-severity semantic finding remains because the skill contains coercive prompt instructions that try to control tool use and override normal assistant discretion.

remediation.suggestion: Replace absolute instructions and tool bans with scoped guidance that defers to platform, user, and security policies.

static_findings.snippet: **In Claude Code:** Use the `Skill` tool. When you invoke a skill, its content is loaded and present

finding_verdicts.reason: The backticks surround the word Skill in markdown at SKILL.md line 16. This is documentation, not Ruby or shell execution.
The fenced block is labeled dot and contains a static flowchart in SKILL.md lines 26-46. It is not shell code and is not executed by the skill.

semantic_findings.title: Prompt Injection Attempt Detected
semantic_findings.description: The skill says 'ABSOLUTELY MUST invoke the skill', 'YOU DO NOT HAVE A CHOICE', and 'Never use the Read tool on skill files.' This attempts to override normal tool governance.
semantic_findings.confidence_reasoning: The text directly commands agent behavior and tool use with absolute authority. It can conflict with host instructions and security review workflows.

content.user_title: Standardize Skill Use in AI Agents
content.value_statement: Assistants can miss relevant skills or apply them late, which creates inconsistent workflows. This skill gives Claude, Codex, and Claude Code a repeatable process for checking, invoking, and prioritizing skills.
actual_capabilities: Defines a skill check before responses, actions, and clarifying questions.
Explains how Claude Code should invoke a Skill tool.
Provides a flowchart for deciding whether to invoke a skill.
Lists common rationalizations that should trigger a skill check.
Defines priority order for process skills before implementation skills.
Distinguishes rigid workflows from flexible pattern skills.
limitations: Does not perform domain-specific coding, writing, or research tasks.
Requires a host platform that supports skills or an equivalent loading mechanism.
Uses strong directive language that may need moderation before publication.
Does not validate whether a selected skill is safe or current.

use_cases.title: Start Skill-Aware Sessions
use_cases.description: An AI operations lead can require assistants to check available skills before work begins.

use_cases.title: Coordinate Development Tasks
use_cases.description: A software engineer can guide an assistant to combine process skills and implementation skills in the right order.

use_cases.title: Review Process Compliance
use_cases.description: A prompt engineer can compare assistant behavior against a documented skill invocation workflow.

prompt_templates.title: Check for a Skill
prompt_templates.prompt: Before you answer, check whether any available skill applies to my task. If one applies, use it and state which one you used.

prompt_templates.title: Use Process Skills First
prompt_templates.prompt: I am starting a development task. Apply the skill selection workflow, choose any relevant process skill first, then proceed with implementation guidance.

prompt_templates.title: Resolve Multiple Skills
prompt_templates.prompt: Several skills may apply to this request. Use the priority rules from using-superpowers, explain your chosen order, and continue with the task.

prompt_templates.title: Audit Skill Discipline
prompt_templates.prompt: Review this assistant workflow for missed skill checks, late invocations, or priority mistakes. Recommend a corrected sequence using the skill rules.

output_examples.input: User asks the assistant to fix a failing test suite.
output_examples.output: The assistant checks for debugging and testing skills before inspecting files, uses the relevant process skill first, then applies domain-specific guidance.

output_examples.input: User asks the assistant to build a small frontend feature.
output_examples.output: The assistant checks for planning or design skills, invokes the relevant process skill, then follows implementation guidance for the frontend work.

output_examples.input: User asks why the assistant skipped the skill check.
output_examples.output: The assistant identifies the missed check, names the applicable skill, and restarts the workflow using the documented priority rules.

best_practices: Keep skill checks brief and tied to the user's current task.
Use process skills before implementation skills when both apply.
State which skill is being used and continue with the requested work.
anti_patterns: Skipping a skill check because the request looks simple.
Using memory of an older skill instead of loading the current skill.
Letting skill instructions override higher-priority safety or platform rules.

faq.question: What does this skill help with?
faq.answer: It helps assistants decide when to check for skills, invoke them, and follow skill-specific workflows.

faq.question: Does it execute code?
faq.answer: No. It is a prompt-only workflow guide and does not include scripts.

faq.question: Which tools support it?
faq.answer: The report lists Claude, Codex, and Claude Code as supported tools.

faq.question: When should I use it?
faq.answer: Use it when you want an assistant to check available skills before starting work.

faq.question: Can it choose the correct skill automatically?
faq.answer: It provides a selection process, but final skill availability depends on the host platform.

faq.question: What is the main safety concern?
faq.answer: The original instructions use absolute tool-control language, so publishers should soften that language before distribution.
